claim: Teichoic acids (TA) are linear phospho-saccharidic polymers and important constituents of the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Teichoic acids (TA) are linear phospho-saccharidic polymers and important constituents of the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria, either bound to the peptidoglycan as wall teichoic acids (WTA) or to the membrane as lipoteichoic acids (LTA).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about TA that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: TA exist in two forms: wall teichoic acids (WTA) bound to peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acids (LTA) bound to the membrane.
source: Teichoic acids (TA) are linear phospho-saccharidic polymers and important constituents of the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria, either bound to the peptidoglycan as wall teichoic acids (WTA) or to the membrane as lipoteichoic acids (LTA).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the two forms of TA based on established knowledge.

claim: The composition of TA varies greatly among different organisms.
source: The composition of TA varies greatly but the presence of both WTA and LTA is highly conserved, hinting at an underlying fundamental function that is distinct from their specific roles in diverse organisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field about TA diversity.

claim: The presence of both WTA and LTA is highly conserved across Gram-positive bacteria.
source: The composition of TA varies greatly but the presence of both WTA and LTA is highly conserved, hinting at an underlying fundamental function that is distinct from their specific roles in diverse organisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis across species, supported by established knowledge.

claim: The conservation of both WTA and LTA suggests an underlying fundamental function distinct from their specific roles in diverse organisms.
source: The composition of TA varies greatly but the presence of both WTA and LTA is highly conserved, hinting at an underlying fundamental function that is distinct from their specific roles in diverse organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation of conservation patterns.

claim: A periplasmic space exists in Streptococcus pneumoniae as observed by cryo-electron microscopy of vitreous sections.
source: We report the observation of a periplasmic space in Streptococcus pneumoniae by cryo-electron microscopy of vitreous sections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CEMOVIS imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: The thickness and appearance of the periplasmic space change upon deletion of genes involved in the attachment of TA.
source: The thickness and appearance of this region change upon deletion of genes involved in the attachment of TA, supporting their role in the maintenance of a periplasmic space in Gram-positive bacteria as a possible universal function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing WT, ΔtacL, and ΔlytR strains by CEMOVIS.

claim: TA play a role in the maintenance of a periplasmic space in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: The thickness and appearance of this region change upon deletion of genes involved in the attachment of TA, supporting their role in the maintenance of a periplasmic space in Gram-positive bacteria as a possible universal function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that deletion of TA-related genes affects periplasmic space structure.

claim: The novel labeling method enabled in-gel analysis of cell fractions.
source: This novel labeling method also enabled in-gel analysis of cell fractions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing gel electrophoresis analysis of labeled TA.

claim: The actual amount of TA per cell can be titrated using the novel labeling method.
source: With this approach, we were able to titrate the actual amount of TA per cell and to determine the ratio of WTA to LTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental titration data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The ratio of WTA to LTA can be determined using the novel labeling method.
source: With this approach, we were able to titrate the actual amount of TA per cell and to determine the ratio of WTA to LTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gel electrophoresis and densitometry analysis.

claim: TA length changes during different growth phases.
source: In addition, we followed the change of TA length during growth phases, and discovered that a mutant devoid of LTA accumulates the membrane-bound polymerized TA precursor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gel electrophoresis of cells harvested at different growth phases.

claim: A mutant devoid of LTA (ΔtacL) accumulates membrane-bound polymerized TA precursor.
source: In addition, we followed the change of TA length during growth phases, and discovered that a mutant devoid of LTA accumulates the membrane-bound polymerized TA precursor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gel electrophoresis and biochemical characterization of the ΔtacL strain.

claim: TA are major components of the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Teichoic acids (TA) are major components of the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of bacterial cell biology.

claim: TA are complex linear polysaccharides attached either to the plasma membrane (LTA) or to the peptidoglycan (WTA).
source: TA are complex linear polysaccharides attached either to the plasma membrane (lipoteichoic acids, LTA) or to the peptidoglycan (PG) (wall teichoic acids, WTA) (Brown et al., 2013; Denapaite et al., 2012; Percy and Gründling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Either WTA or LTA are dispensable in some laboratory conditions for the growth of Bacillus subtilis.
source: Either WTA or LTA are dispensable in some laboratory conditions for the growth of Bacillus subtilis (D'Elia et al., 2006a; Schirner et al., 2009) or Staphylococcus aureus (D'Elia et al., 2006b; Oku et al., 2009), but at least one type must be present (Schirner et al., 2009; Oku et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Either WTA or LTA are dispensable in some laboratory conditions for the growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
source: Either WTA or LTA are dispensable in some laboratory conditions for the growth of Bacillus subtilis (D'Elia et al., 2006a; Schirner et al., 2009) or Staphylococcus aureus (D'Elia et al., 2006b; Oku et al., 2009), but at least one type must be present (Schirner et al., 2009; Oku et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: At least one type of TA (either WTA or LTA) must be present in B. subtilis and S. aureus.
source: Either WTA or LTA are dispensable in some laboratory conditions for the growth of Bacillus subtilis (D'Elia et al., 2006a; Schirner et al., 2009) or Staphylococcus aureus (D'Elia et al., 2006b; Oku et al., 2009), but at least one type must be present (Schirner et al., 2009; Oku et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, LTA are dispensable.
source: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, LTA are dispensable (Heß et al., 2017), and reduced amount of WTA is tolerated (Minhas et al., 2023) (strains totally devoid of WTA have not been characterized yet due to partial redundancy of WTA attachment enzymes).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Reduced amounts of WTA are tolerated in S. pneumoniae.
source: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, LTA are dispensable (Heß et al., 2017), and reduced amount of WTA is tolerated (Minhas et al., 2023) (strains totally devoid of WTA have not been characterized yet due to partial redundancy of WTA attachment enzymes).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Strains totally devoid of WTA have not been characterized yet in S. pneumoniae due to partial redundancy of WTA attachment enzymes.
source: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, LTA are dispensable (Heß et al., 2017), and reduced amount of WTA is tolerated (Minhas et al., 2023) (strains totally devoid of WTA have not been characterized yet due to partial redundancy of WTA attachment enzymes).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of knowledge and experimental limitations.

claim: TA participate in numerous cellular processes including cell wall elongation and hydrolysis, cell division, transport processes, cation homeostasis, resistance to antimicrobial peptides, and interactions with the environment or the host.
source: TA participate in numerous cellular processes such as cell wall elongation and hydrolysis, cell division, transport processes, cation homeostasis, resistance to antimicrobial peptides, and interactions with the environment or the host.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous studies in the field.

claim: A region between the cytoplasmic membrane and the cell wall was proposed to be a periplasmic space in Gram-positive bacteria (B. subtilis, S. aureus, Enterococcus gallinarum, and Streptococcus gordonii) by cryo-electron microscopy of vitreous sections.
source: In studies of Gram-positive bacteria (B. subtilis, S. aureus, Enterococcus gallinarum, and Streptococcus gordonii) by cryo-electron microscopy of vitreous sections (CEMOVIS; Dubochet et al., 1988), a region between the cytoplasmic membrane and the cell wall was proposed to be a periplasmic space (Matias and Beveridge, 2007; Matias and Beveridge, 2008; Zuber et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CEMOVIS studies.

claim: TA may play a role in maintaining a periplasmic space that is isotonic with the cytoplasm.
source: A most interesting speculation is the possible role of TA in maintaining this periplasmic space, so that it would be isotonic with the cytoplasm (Figure 1A; Erickson, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis cited from Erickson, 2021 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In most organisms, LTA and WTA have different compositions and are assembled and exported by different pathways.
source: In most organisms, LTA and WTA have different compositions and are assembled and exported by different pathways (Brown et al., 2013; Percy and Gründling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TA of streptococci of the mitis group are products of the same biosynthetic pathway.
source: TA of streptococci of the mitis group, such as S. pneumoniae, are particular in two ways: LTA and WTA are products of the same biosynthetic pathway and are therefore of very similar composition, and they are uniquely decorated by phosphocholine residues (Figure 1B; Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: LTA and WTA in streptococci of the mitis group are of very similar composition.
source: TA of streptococci of the mitis group, such as S. pneumoniae, are particular in two ways: LTA and WTA are products of the same biosynthetic pathway and are therefore of very similar composition, and they are uniquely decorated by phosphocholine residues (Figure 1B; Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: TA of streptococci of the mitis group are uniquely decorated by phosphocholine residues.
source: TA of streptococci of the mitis group, such as S. pneumoniae, are particular in two ways: LTA and WTA are products of the same biosynthetic pathway and are therefore of very similar composition, and they are uniquely decorated by phosphocholine residues (Figure 1B; Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: 13-16 different choline-binding proteins are anchored to the cell envelope of S. pneumoniae by interaction of their choline-binding domain to phosphocholine residues.
source: The role of TA in the pneumococcus is also critical because 13–16 different proteins (choline-binding proteins) are anchored to the cell envelope by the interaction of their choline-binding domain to phosphocholine residues (Maestro and Sanz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The functions of choline-binding proteins are diverse, including cell wall hydrolases and virulence factors.
source: The functions of the choline-binding proteins are diverse, several of them are acting on the cell wall itself as hydrolases such as LytA and LytB, others are virulence factors mediating interactions with the host and its immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about choline-binding proteins in S. pneumoniae.

claim: S. pneumoniae has a strict nutritional requirement for choline, which is solely incorporated in its TA.
source: The pneumococcus has a strict nutritional requirement for choline, which is solely incorporated in its TA (Tomasz, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Numerous derivatives can substitute for choline in S. pneumoniae, as long as the hydroxyl group is present and the amine substituents are not too bulky.
source: However, numerous derivatives can substitute for choline, as long as the hydroxyl group is present and the amine substituents are not too bulky (Badger, 1944).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The pneumococcal repeating unit of TA consists of a pseudo-pentasaccharide with a specific structure.
source: The pneumococcal repeating unit of TA consists of a pseudo-pentasaccharide ((→4)-6-O-P-Cho-α-D-GalpNAc-(1→3)-6-O-P-Cho-β-D-GalpNAc-(1→1)-Rib-ol-5-P-(O→6)-β-D-Glcp-(1→3)-AATGalp-(1→)) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Fischer, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural characterization and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In LTA, the AATGalp of the first subunit is β-(1→6)-linked to the glucose of a mono-glucosyl-diacyl-glycerol.
source: In LTA, the acetamido-4-amino-6-deoxygalactopyranose (AATGalp) of the first subunit is β-(1→6)-linked to the glucose of a mono-glucosyl-diacyl-glycerol (DGlcp-DAG) (Gisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural characterization.

claim: In WTA, the first AATGalp is thought to be α-linked via a phosphodiester to position 6 of the PG N-acetyl muramic acid.
source: In WTA, the first AATGalp is thought to be α-linked via a phosphodiester to position 6 of the PG N-acetyl muramic acid, as in WTA of other species, although this labile linkage has never been experimentally observed in S. pneumoniae (Fischer, 1997; Bui et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on analogy to other species, with citations noting the lack of direct experimental evidence.

claim: The basic unit of TA is intracellularly synthesized at the plasma membrane onto the carrier lipid undecaprenyl pyrophosphate by a succession of glycosyl- and phosphotransferases.
source: Like other surface polysaccharides such as the PG or the capsule, the basic unit is intracellularly synthesized at the plasma membrane onto the carrier lipid undecaprenyl pyrophosphate by a succession of glycosyl- and phosphotransferases (Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The basic unit precursor is thought to be flipped across the membrane by the flippase TacF.
source: The basic unit precursor is then thought to be flipped across the membrane by the flippase TacF (spr1150) to allow elongation of the TA polymers at the cell surface by the polymerase TarP (spr1222) (Damjanovic et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2017; Gibson and Veening, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Elongation of TA polymers at the cell surface is performed by the polymerase TarP.
source: The basic unit precursor is then thought to be flipped across the membrane by the flippase TacF (spr1150) to allow elongation of the TA polymers at the cell surface by the polymerase TarP (spr1222) (Damjanovic et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2017; Gibson and Veening, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A phosphotransferase can anchor the TA polymer onto the PG to yield WTA.
source: Once on the external surface of the membrane, the polymerized precursors can undergo two fates (Figure 1B). A phosphotransferase can anchor the polymer onto the PG to yield WTA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WTA biosynthesis, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: A glycosyltransferase can transfer the TA polymer to DGlcp-DAG to form LTA.
source: Alternatively, a glycosyltransferase can transfer the polymer to DGlcp-DAG to form LTA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LTA biosynthesis.

claim: The phosphotransferase attaching WTA is thought to be LytR.
source: The phosphotransferase attaching WTA is thought to be LytR (spr1759) (Minhas et al., 2023), although LytR and the two homologous enzymes Cps2A (spr 0314) and Psr (spr1226) that form the LCP (LytR-Cps2A-Psr) family may exhibit some redundancy (Kawai et al., 2011; Eberhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LytR and the two homologous enzymes Cps2A and Psr that form the LCP family may exhibit some redundancy.
source: The phosphotransferase attaching WTA is thought to be LytR (spr1759) (Minhas et al., 2023), although LytR and the two homologous enzymes Cps2A (spr 0314) and Psr (spr1226) that form the LCP (LytR-Cps2A-Psr) family may exhibit some redundancy (Kawai et al., 2011; Eberhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The glycosyltransferase producing LTA was found to be TacL.
source: The glycosyltransferase producing LTA was found to be TacL (spr1702), since the purification procedure normally yielding LTA produced no detectable TA compounds from a ΔtacL strain (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Competence in S. pneumoniae is accompanied by an increase in the amount of WTA dependent on the presence of LytR.
source: Notably, competence, the process allowing incorporation of DNA from the extracellular environment, was found to be accompanied by an increase of the amount of WTA dependent on the presence of the phosphotransferase LytR, whose expression is upregulated during competence (Minhas et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Autolysis in S. pneumoniae depends on the relative abundance of LTA and WTA.
source: In contrast, autolysis, which occurs during the stationary phase of planktonic cultures and is mostly driven by the PG amidase and choline-binding protein LytA, was shown to depend on the relative abundance of LTA and WTA (Flores-Kim et al., 2019), modulated by the phosphodiesterase WhyD that releases TA from the PG (Flores-Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The phosphodiesterase WhyD releases TA from the PG.
source: In contrast, autolysis, which occurs during the stationary phase of planktonic cultures and is mostly driven by the PG amidase and choline-binding protein LytA, was shown to depend on the relative abundance of LTA and WTA (Flores-Kim et al., 2019), modulated by the phosphodiesterase WhyD that releases TA from the PG (Flores-Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: WTA are attached to the C-6 hydroxyl of N-acetyl muramic acids in the PG of S. pneumoniae.
source: WTA are attached to the C-6 hydroxyl of N-acetyl muramic acids in the PG of S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WTA attachment.

claim: The C-6 position of N-acetyl muramic acid is the site of O-acetylation by Adr.
source: This position is also the site of O-acetylation by Adr (Crisóstomo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The C-6 hydroxyl of N-acetyl muramic acid is often assumed to be the site of capsule attachment via a phosphodiester linkage.
source: The same hydroxyl is also often assumed to be the site of attachment of the capsule by a similar phosphodiester linkage (Eberhardt et al., 2012), although the serotype 2 capsule has now been found to be attached via a direct glycosidic bond to the C-6 position of PG N-acetyl glucosamine (Larson and Yother, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies, with a note that this assumption has been challenged for serotype 2.

claim: The serotype 2 capsule is attached via a direct glycosidic bond to the C-6 position of PG N-acetyl glucosamine.
source: The same hydroxyl is also often assumed to be the site of attachment of the capsule by a similar phosphodiester linkage (Eberhardt et al., 2012), although the serotype 2 capsule has now been found to be attached via a direct glycosidic bond to the C-6 position of PG N-acetyl glucosamine (Larson and Yother, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There is cross-talk between TA attachment to the PG, O-acetylation and capsule attachment.
source: There is thus certainly a cross-talk between TA attachment to the PG, O-acetylation and capsule attachment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these processes compete for the same attachment site.

claim: CEMOVIS reveals the existence of a periplasm in WT S. pneumoniae as evidenced by a light region between the plasma membrane and the cell wall.
source: As in other bacterial species, CEMOVIS reveals the existence of a periplasm in WT S. pneumoniae, as evidenced by a light region observed between the plasma membrane and the cell wall (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental CEMOVIS data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within the periplasmic space, a single dark line runs parallel to the membrane, described as a granular layer.
source: Within this light region, a single dark line runs parallel to the membrane. This observation in S. pneumoniae supports the idea that a periplasmic space exists in Gram-positive bacteria, and that this space contains organized material, which was previously described as a granular layer (Zuber et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental CEMOVIS data and citation to a previous study.

claim: The granular layer completely disappears in ΔlytR and ΔtacL cells.
source: Strikingly, the granular layer present in the WT strain completely disappears in ΔlytR and ΔtacL cells (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental CEMOVIS data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of TacL, the thickness of the periplasmic space is significantly reduced by (34 ± 5)% (SE) compared to the WT strain.
source: In the absence of TacL, the thickness of the periplasmic space is significantly reduced by (34 ± 5)% (SE) compared to that of the WT strain (Table 1), supporting the idea that LTA occupy the periplasmic space.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements from CEMOVIS images presented in Table 1.

claim: The absence of LytR induces a significant reduction of the periplasm thickness ((29 ± 5)% (SE)).
source: Similarly, the absence of LytR induces a significant reduction of the periplasm thickness ((29 ± 5)% (SE), Table 1), suggesting that WTA also participate in the maintenance of this region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements from CEMOVIS images presented in Table 1.

claim: WTA participate in the maintenance of the periplasmic space.
source: Similarly, the absence of LytR induces a significant reduction of the periplasm thickness ((29 ± 5)% (SE), Table 1), suggesting that WTA also participate in the maintenance of this region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that deletion of lytR reduces periplasmic space thickness.

claim: The thickness of the periplasmic spaces in ΔtacL and ΔlytR strains does not differ significantly from each other.
source: The thickness of the periplasmic spaces in ΔtacL and ΔlytR strains does not differ significantly from each other.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of CEMOVIS measurements.

claim: The cell wall thickness is significantly reduced by (17 ± 5)% (SE) in the absence of TacL.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant reduction of the cell wall thickness of (17 ± 5)% (SE) or (36 ± 4)% (SE) in the absence of TacL or LytR, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements from CEMOVIS images.

claim: The cell wall thickness is significantly reduced by (36 ± 4)% (SE) in the absence of LytR.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant reduction of the cell wall thickness of (17 ± 5)% (SE) or (36 ± 4)% (SE) in the absence of TacL or LytR, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements from CEMOVIS images.

claim: The reduction in cell wall thickness is more pronounced in ΔlytR cells compared to ΔtacL cells.
source: Consistent with the fact that WTA are covalently linked to the PG, the reduction in the cell wall thickness is more pronounced in ΔlytR cells compared to ΔtacL cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental measurements and the known covalent linkage of WTA to PG.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy analysis of sectioned stained freeze-substituted resin-embedded samples did not reveal measurable differences between the cell wall of the WT and mutant strains.
source: In contrast to the CEMOVIS method, transmission electron microscopy analysis of sectioned stained freeze-substituted resin-embedded samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) did not reveal measurable differences between the cell wall of the WT and mutant strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental TEM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: TA insertion occurs at mid-cell in WT S. pneumoniae.
source: As expected, TA insertion occurs at mid-cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enriched aCho incorporation was detected at midcell in ΔtacL cells.
source: Although the morphology of ΔtacL cells is altered, with pointy poles and some expanded and shrunk cells, enriched aCho incorporation was also detected at midcell.
evidence: This is supported by experimental fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: In the ΔlytR strain, the 5-min incubation with aCho yielded only a weak mid-cell labeling in few cells.
source: In the ΔlytR strain, in contrast to the WT parental and ΔtacL strains, the 5-min incubation with aCho yielded only a weak mid-cell labeling in few cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the three strains (WT, ΔtacL, ΔlytR), TA were mostly inserted at mid-cell, where the PG is assembled.
source: In the three strains, TA were mostly inserted at mid-cell, where the PG is assembled (Trouve et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data and citation to a previous study.

claim: Some TA localizations were detected elsewhere at the cell surface in all three strains.
source: However, some localizations were also detected elsewhere at the cell surface in all three strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data.

claim: The localization patterns of newly incorporated TA are mostly that of WTA, since this distribution is preserved in sacculi preparations.
source: The localization patterns of newly incorporated TA observed in these experiments are mostly that of WTA, since this distribution is preserved in sacculi preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental dSTORM data of sacculi shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In WT cells, the separated banded pattern expected from the insertion of unlabeled TA at the division site is observed after a chase.
source: In the WT strain, the separated banded pattern expected from the insertion of unlabeled TA at the division site is observed, mirroring the patterns produced by PG labeling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data from pulse-chase experiments.

claim: In ΔtacL cells, labeled TA can be seen over the whole new cell surface that is generated during the pulse and the first 15 min of chase.
source: In contrast, in ΔtacL cells, labeled TA can be seen over the whole new cell surface that is generated during the pulse and the first 15 min of chase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: An unlabeled region is visible at mid-cell in ΔtacL cells only after 35 min of chase.
source: An unlabeled region is visible at mid-cell in ΔtacL cells only after 35 min of chase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The chased pattern of labeled PG in the ΔtacL strain is not affected and is similar to that in WT.
source: The chased pattern of labeled PG in the ΔtacL strain is not affected and is similar to that in WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dSTORM data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: LTA-containing membranes of S. pneumoniae sediment at low centrifugal speed.
source: Since we were able to fluorescently label TA, we thought it would allow simpler in-gel analysis. WT cells were cultured over two generations in C-medium devoid of choline but supplemented with 200 µM aCho. Cells having thus metabolically incorporated aCho were lyzed by overnight digestion of the cell wall with lysozyme, mutanolysin and recombinant LytA. The aCho was coupled to a DBCO-fluorescent Alexa dye (AF488) by SPAAC click reaction during the lysis incubation. The lysates were then cleared of debris by a low-speed centrifugation at 10,000 × g, and ultracentrifugation of the supernatant at 100,000 × g was subsequently performed to separate the membrane from the soluble fraction. Since at this stage the TA were fluorescently labeled, we were surprised to find more fluorescence in the low-speed pellet than in the pellet resulting from the ultracentrifugation.
evidence: This is an unexpected experimental observation from the fractionation procedure.

claim: The pattern expected from labeled WTA is a set of poorly resolved bands with low electrophoretic mobility.
source: Analysis of the soluble fraction (the supernatant) by SDS–PAGE showed the pattern expected from labeled WTA migrating as a set of poorly resolved bands with low electrophoretic mobility, as in typical Alcian blue-stained gels (Flores-Kim et al., 2019; Flores-Kim et al., 2022; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The pattern expected from labeled LTA is a ladder of well-resolved bands with a greater electrophoretic mobility than the WTA.
source: The pattern expected from labeled LTA, a ladder of well-resolved bands with a greater electrophoretic mobility than the WTA, was observed chiefly in the low-speed pellet.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 2 min at 20,000 × g were sufficient to sediment most of the LTA.
source: Centrifugation of cells lysates with labeled TA at different speeds confirmed that 2 min at 20,000 × g were sufficient to sediment most of the LTA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental centrifugation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The total amount of TA choline residues per cell is about (12.5 ± 1.5) × 10^6.
source: The total amount of TA choline residues per cell can therefore be estimated to be about (12.5 ± 1.5) × 106.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: The number of TA molecules per cell is about 10^6.
source: Assuming that the major species of TA consists of 6 repeating units, as determined previously (Gisch et al., 2013; Bui et al., 2012), with each unit comprising about two choline residues, the number of TA molecules per cell is about 106.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data and assumptions about TA structure, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Labeled choline residues incorporated into LTAs account for 15 ± 5% of the TA choline residues.
source: Labeled choline residues incorporated into LTAs were found to account for 15 ± 5% of the TA choline residues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification from gel electrophoresis data.

claim: LTA and WTA represent roughly 15 and 85% of pneumococcal TA, respectively.
source: Assuming that the amount of polymerized TA precursors is negligible, and that size distribution is similar for LTA and WTA, LTA and WTA represent roughly 15 and 85% of pneumococcal TA, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental quantification data with stated assumptions.

claim: Longer species of LTA can be observed at later stages of growth.
source: Remarkably, longer species of LTA can be observed at later stages of growth (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The most abundant form of LTA consists of 6 repeating units during exponential phase.
source: Assuming that the most abundant form consists of 6 repeating units (Gisch et al., 2013), the 5- and 7-unit species are the next most abundant species, and traces of the 8- and 9-unit species can be detected during the exponential phase of growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data and citation to a previous study.

claim: During late culture phases, longer LTA species become more abundant with up to 17 identifiable units.
source: Later during the culture, although the 6-unit species remains the most abundant and the 5-unit is detected at level comparable as earlier in the culture, longer species become more abundant with up to 17 identifiable units.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: The size distribution of LTA in late culture appears to be bimodal with a first group of species consisting of 5–11 units, and a second group of longer forms where the most abundant one contains 15 units.
source: Surprisingly, the size distribution appears to be bimodal with a first group of species consisting of 5–11 units, and a second group of longer forms where the most abundant one contains 15 units.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: There was no significant difference in LTA length distribution between WT and ΔlytA strains.
source: There was no significant difference between the strains with and without LytA (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data comparing the two strains.

claim: Although WT cells lyse, their WTA and LTA are not degraded and remain unchanged in the medium.
source: The ΔlytA did not lyse spontaneously, but a similar amount of TA with the same distribution was obtained from the lysing lytA+ culture. Thus, although the WT cells lyse, their WTA and LTA are not degraded and remain unchanged in the medium.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental gel electrophoresis data comparing lysing and non-lysing cultures.

claim: No modification of the pulse-labeled TA could be detected during the chase time in WT cells.
source: We also monitored the fate of the labeled species during a chase period of further growth following a 5-min labeling pulse of WT cells, mirroring the dSTORM observations. No modification of the pulse-labeled TA could be detected during the chase time, whether the growth, labeling pulse and chase were performed in BHI or C-medium and supplemented with yeast extract (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Labeled TA found in the pellet of ΔtacL lysates are indistinguishable from LTA when analyzed by gel electrophoresis.
source: WTA and LTA were examined in a strain devoid of TacL, which is thought to be responsible for the attachment of LTA to membrane glycolipids (Figure 6A). Labeled TA were found in the pellet, and when analyzed by gel electrophoresis were indistinguishable from LTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The sedimented TA in ΔtacL cells are membrane-bound precursors still attached to the undecaprenyl pyrophosphate lipid carrier.
source: After double checking that the strain was indeed deleted for the tacL gene, we hypothesized that the sedimented TA could be membrane-bound precursors still attached to the undecaprenyl pyrophosphate lipid carrier.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and subsequent biochemical characterization.

claim: Pulse-labeled LTA-like bands disappeared during a chase in ΔtacL cells.
source: In support of this idea, pulse-labeled LTA-like bands disappeared during a chase (Figure 6B), as would be expected if these compounds were precursors being transformed into WTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The pyrophosphate linkage in TA precursors is labile at low pH and high temperature.
source: The pyrophosphate linkage in the PG precursor lipid II is labile at low pH and high temperature (Higashi et al., 1967). Reasoning that the same should be true for the TA precursor, we incubated the sedimented fraction from the WT and ΔtacL strain at 99°C at either pH 8 or pH 4.2. The TA sedimented from the ΔtacL lysate were degraded at both pH, whereas those from the parental strain were still detected (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citation to a previous study on lipid II.

claim: P. aeruginosa colicin M can hydrolyze labeled sedimented TA from ΔtacL cells.
source: P. aeruginosa colicin M could indeed hydrolyze labeled sedimented TA from ΔtacL cells, whereas it was inactive on labeled LTA from WT cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TacL is the glycosyltransferase responsible for the attachment of TA to the membrane glycolipids.
source: The combined results show that TacL is indeed the glycosyltransferase responsible for the attachment of TA to the membrane glycolipids (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from this study and citation to a previous study.

claim: In the absence of TacL, membrane-bound TA remain present in abundance in the form of undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate-attached precursors.
source: Moreover, they reveal that in the absence of TacL, membrane-bound TA remain present in abundance in the form of undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate-attached precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from biochemical characterization of the ΔtacL strain.

claim: LTA in the WT strain and membrane-bound precursors in the ΔtacL strain are located on the outer side of the plasma membrane.
source: LTA in the WT strain or membrane-bound precursors in the ΔtacL strain were equally labeled before and after lysis, like WTA. In contrast, cytoplasmic azido-phosphocholine was only labeled after lysis, demonstrating that the DBCO-AF488 dye is membrane impermeant. These observations are in agreement with the polymerization of TA taking place at the cell surface (Gibson and Veening, 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from click-labeling before and after lysis, shown in Figure 6F, and citation to a previous study.

claim: In the WT strain, labeled WTA represent ~80% of the total labeled TA.
source: In the WT strain, labeled WTA in this particular experiment was found to represent ~80% of the total labeled TA, whereas in the ΔlytR strain, this proportion decreased to ~40%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental densitometry data from gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the ΔlytR strain, labeled WTA represent ~40% of the total labeled TA.
source: In the WT strain, labeled WTA in this particular experiment was found to represent ~80% of the total labeled TA, whereas in the ΔlytR strain, this proportion decreased to ~40%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental densitometry data from gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of WTA to LTA amounts is decreased about five to sevenfold in the absence of LytR.
source: Thus, the ratio of WTA to LTA amounts is decreased about five to sevenfold in the absence of LytR.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental densitometry data.

claim: The thinning of the periplasmic space and disappearance of the granular layer in strains with diminished amounts of either WTA or LTA support Erickson's hypothesis that a periplasmic space is maintained by the physical properties of WTA and LTA.
source: The thinning of the periplasmic space and disappearance of the granular layer in strains with diminished amounts of either WTA (ΔlytR) or LTA (ΔtacL) support Erickson's hypothesis that a periplasmic space is maintained by the physical properties of WTA emanating from the PG layer and LTA springing from the membrane Erickson, 2021.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental CEMOVIS data and citation to Erickson's hypothesis.

claim: The appearance of the cell envelope of S. gordonii and S. pneumoniae are similar by CEMOVIS, despite different TA compositions.
source: In this framework, it is also striking that the appearance of the cell envelope of S. gordonii (Zuber et al., 2006) and S. pneumoniae are so similar, despite the fact that the composition of their TA are very different (Denapaite et al., 2012; Park et al., 2020; Lima et al., 2019), lending credence to a fundamental function of TA stemming from their general physico-chemical properties, rather than from specific molecular interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of CEMOVIS data with citations to previous studies on TA composition.

claim: The surface density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is about 3.3 × 10^16 molecule⋅m^−2 or one LTA chain per 30 nm^2.
source: The surface density of LTA would therefore be 3.3 × 1016 molecule⋅m–2 or one LTA chain per 30 nm2.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data and geometric assumptions about cell size.

claim: The density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is lower than that calculated for LTA from Staphylococcus aureus (one chain per 5 nm^2).
source: This density value is lower than that of one chain per 5 nm2 calculated for LTA from Staphylococcus aureus based on the ratio of LTA to membrane lipids (Erickson, 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with a calculation cited from a previous study.

claim: The density values of LTA in S. pneumoniae and S. aureus are probably compatible with the polymer brush model.
source: Although both density values are rough estimates, they likely require volume exclusion to accommodate TA chains at the membrane surface and are probably compatible with the polymer brush model.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on calculated density values and theoretical models.

claim: In WT cells, production of WTA and LTA are competing pathways that rapidly consume the undecaprenyl-linked polymerized TA precursors.
source: It is most likely that in WT cells, production of WTA and LTA are competing pathways as the two polymers share the same composition, that rapidly consumes the undecaprenyl-linked polymerized TA precursors, whereas these precursors accumulate in the ΔtacL strain (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and biochemical characterization.

claim: The slower turnover of undecaprenyl-linked TA in the ΔtacL strain allows the cell wall incorporation of labeled WTA during the chase, several minutes after the aCho has been removed from the medium.
source: The slower turnover of the undecaprenyl-linked TA in the ΔtacL strain allows the cell wall incorporation of labeled WTA during the chase, several minutes after the aCho has been removed from the medium.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental dSTORM and gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments.

claim: The observation by CEMOVIS that the cell envelope architecture is altered in ΔtacL cells indicates that undecaprenyl-attached TA precursors cannot fully replace the function of mature LTA.
source: The observation by CEMOVIS that the cell envelope architecture is altered in ΔtacL cells, with a thinner periplasmic space devoid of granular layer (Figure 1), indicates that if some functional replacement occurs, it is not complete.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental CEMOVIS data.

claim: The physical properties of the undecaprenyl chain may restrict the presence and function of undecaprenyl-linked TA precursors to sites of cell wall assembly.
source: It has been proposed previously that the physical properties of the undecaprenyl chain underlie the localization of the PG precursor lipid II at the sites of cell wall assembly, which occurs at sites of maximal membrane curvature (Calvez et al., 2019). The same reasoning would restrict the presence, and thus the function, of the undecaprenyl-linked TA precursors to sites of cell wall assembly were they can be incorporated into WTA or true LTA.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on analogy to lipid II localization, with citation to a previous study.

claim: It is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in previous studies during a clarification step of cell lysates.
source: However, it is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in these experiments during a clarification step of cell lysates, suggesting that the reported ratio of LTA to WTA were underestimated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of low-speed sedimentation of LTA-containing membranes.

claim: The reported ratio of LTA to WTA in previous studies were likely underestimated.
source: However, it is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in these experiments during a clarification step of cell lysates, suggesting that the reported ratio of LTA to WTA were underestimated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of low-speed sedimentation of LTA-containing membranes.
